Participants. 80 adults participated online using Amazon's Mechanical Turk (Mage = 46.4 years, range = 22-76, 52 females).
All participants were native English speakers residing in the United States and received a nominal payment for their participation.
As specified in the preregistration, participants were required to pass simple catch questions to ensure they were attending to the task.

At the beginning of the study, participants were told that three researchers had traveled to a city they had not previously visited, and that the researchers' job was to make notes about some of the things they encountered while they explored the city.
Participants were then informed that they would hear about some of the specific encounters of the researchers, and they would be asked some questions.

On each trial, participants were told about one of the specific entities the researchers had encountered on one of the days they were exploring the city (e.g., "One day, the researchers came across an actor").

On the presence question, participants were asked whether they thought the specific category member would have the property for that trial (e.g., after being told the researchers had met an actor, they were asked: "Do you think they portray characters?"
On the certainty question, participants were asked if they were certain that the specific category member encountered would have the property (e.g., "Are you certain that they portray characters?"

Participants completed 32 trials, involving 16 categories and two properties per category: a form property (e.g., portraying characters for an actor) and a generic property (e.g., having an agent for an actor).

In each domain participants were certain form properties would be present in category members from that domain: for the artifacts (76%, p < .001), events (74%, p < .001), places (75%, p < .001), and social categories (61%, p = .009).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Do form and generic properties of familiar kinds license true generics?
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Hypothesis: Both form properties and generic properties license a true generic. For example, for the concept tire, participants will accept a generic for a form property (e.g., "Tires are round") and for a generic property (e.g., "Tires are black").
table.design_dependent_variables: On each trial, participants will be presented with a generic statement about a form property (e.g., "Tires are round") or a generic statement about a generic property (e.g., "Tires are black"). They will be asked whether the statement strikes them as true (yes/no response options). Participants will complete 32 trials involving 16 different familiar kinds-four artifacts, four events, four institutions, and four social kinds. For each kind, a form property and a generic property of the kind will be tested. Trial order will be randomized.
table.study_design_overview: This experiment will be a within-subjects experiment.
table.statistical_tests: I will investigate whether the average endorsements (yes responses) of the generic statements across all trials is greater that chance for both the form properties and the generic properties (both one sample student's t-tests, two-tailed, significance threshold: p<0.05). I predict that they will be.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
The study will include some easy catch questions, primarily designed to filter out bots, as well as participants who are not paying attention to the contents of the study. First, at the beginning of the study participants will be presented with a simple exchange between two characters (Liam and Emma). They will then be asked to type in an open textbox who Liam was talking to. It will be made clear to participants that the purpose of this question is to filter out bots. Participants who fail this question will be thanked for their time on the subsequent display, and they will not complete the study.

Second, two easy catch questions will be included in the study (e.g., "Is a square a four-sided shape"). Participants who fail either or both of these questions will not complete the remainder of the study and will be excluded.

Third, participants will be required to correctly recall some of the kinds of things they had just been asked about. Participants who fail this question will be excluded.

Finally, participants will be required to have English as one of their first languages to participate in the study. All participants will complete a language comprehension task prior to the study to ensure they are fluent in English. Participants will read a short passage and will answer two questions about the passage to test their comprehension of English. Participants who do not answer both questions correctly will be thanked for their time on the subsequent display, and they will not complete the study. Participants will be asked whether English is one of their first languages and they will be required to confirm that it is in order to be included in the participant sample.

Excluded participants will not count towards the target sample sizes.
table.sample_size: 80 participants will be recruited. Sample sizes are based on a power analysis of pilot data, which showed a large effect size (for our primary analysis, Cohen's d>1). I conservatively target 80 participants, the sample required to detect this effect at 99% power.

table.title: Does the central form of a novel kind concept activate certainty beliefs?
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Hypothesis: When a property of a novel kind is represented via the central form of the kind concept, a certainty belief is immediately licensed whereby people who possess this concept will express psychological certainty that the property will be possessed by a newly encountered member of the kind (call this the Certainty Signature). For example, if people represent serving milk as part of the central form of the concept 'bozon,' then when they subsequently encounter an instance of the kind bozons, they will initially be certain the bozon will serve milk.
table.design_dependent_variables: Participants will be told that some researchers are exploring a remote island. On each trial, participants will be introduced to a new kind of thing (e.g., a place called a 'bozon'). Participants will then be told about a property of the kind (e.g., serving milk) in one of two conditions (see Q4). On test, they will be told that the researchers have encountered another instance of the kind (e.g., another bozon). Participants will then be asked a presence question followed by a certainty question. On the presence question, participants will be asked whether they think the previously introduced property will be present in the instance (e.g., "Do you think it is serves milk?"). On the certainty question, participants will be asked whether they are certain that the property will be present in the instance (e.g., "Are you certain that it serves milk?").
table.study_design_overview: There will be two conditions, a form condition and a generic condition. In the form condition, participants will be introduced to the property with evidence that it is part of the central form of that kind concept (e.g., "serving milk is part of being a bozon. It's what makes a bozon a bozon"). In the generic condition, participants will be introduced to the property with evidence that it is a generic property, but not part of the kind concept's central form (e.g., "Bozons serve milk, but serving milk is not part of being a bozon").
table.statistical_tests:
I will investigate whether the average endorsements of the certainty belief (yes responses to the certainty question) across all trials is greater in the form condition vs the generic condition (two samples student's t-test, two-tailed, significance threshold: p<0.05). I predict that it will be. 

Furthermore, given these are categorical responses, I plan to run a mixed effects logistic regression using the lme4 package in R in order to explore the effects of condition, item, trial order, age, and gender on the likelihood of endorsing the certainty belief, with subject as a random intercept. I predict a positive coefficient for condition.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
The study will include some easy catch questions, primarily designed to filter out bots, as well as participants who are not paying attention to the contents of the study. First, at the beginning of the study participants will be presented with a simple exchange between two characters (Liam and Emma). They will then be asked to type in an open textbox who Liam was talking to. It will be made clear to participants that the purpose of this question is to filter out bots. Participants who fail this question will be thanked for their time on the subsequent display, and they will not complete the study.

Second, four easy catch questions will be included in the study. Two of these questions will be trivially easy questions unrelated to the study content (e.g., "Is a square a four-sided shape?"; failed response = no). Two of the questions will ask the certainty question of a property which was not introduced to participants, and so they could not possibly be certain that it will be present in an instance (e.g., of animal called a liff, participants will be asked "Are you certain that it is green?" even though they were never told about the color of the animal; failed response = yes). Participants who fail any of these questions will be excluded and not considered for data analysis.

Third, participants will be required to correctly recall some of the kinds of things they had just been asked about. Participants who fail this question will be excluded.

Finally, participants will be required to have English as one of their first languages to participate in the study. All participants will complete a language comprehension task prior to the study to ensure they are fluent in English. Participants will read a short passage and will answer two questions about the passage to test their comprehension of English. Participants who do not answer both questions correctly will be thanked for their time on the subsequent display, and they will not complete the study. Participants will be asked whether English is one of their first languages and they will be required to confirm that it is in order to be included in the participant sample.

In addition to these exclusions, participants who have recently completed a similar study will not be permitted to complete the present study. 

Excluded participants will not count towards the target sample sizes.
table.sample_size: 40 participants will be recruited per condition. Sample sizes are based on a power analysis of pilot data, which showed a large effect size (for our primary analysis, Cohen's d>1). I conservatively target 40 participants per condition, the sample required to detect this effect at 99% power.
table.additional_comments:
I predict that in both the form condition and the generic condition, the percentage of trials on which participants judge that the property is present in a new instance of the kind-their answers to the presence question-will be greater than chance (both one sample t-tests, chance = 50% of trials, two-tailed, significance threshold: p<0.05). 

At the end of the study, all participants will complete a second phase of the experiment, called the form measurement phase. This phase of the experiment will probe how participants had actually encoded the properties used in the main phase of the experiment. Specifically, did they encode them as form properties? For each property, I will investigate whether participants believe the property licenses a criterion/signature of central form. For example: "Recall that in one of the scenarios, you read about "bozons." Did you think that serving milk is part of being a bozon (i.e., one of those things that makes a bozon a bozon)?" It is predicted that the average certainty-belief endorsement will be higher for the properties participants indicated they had encoded as form properties, than those which they had not encoded as form properties (as indicated by their answers for that property in the form property measurement phase; paired samples student's t-test, two-tailed, significance threshold: p<0.05).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. text.text: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified.
Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty.

On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs.
The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief.
In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts.
While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties.
In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts.

As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept's central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept's central form.
These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts.

Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

It captures our intuition about what makes a restaurant a restaurant.
Likewise, houses are for living in, architects design buildings, dogs bark, triangles have three sides, watches tell time, weddings involve a union of people.

No matter the concept, drawn from any domain, a subset of properties can be identified that captures its conceptual identity, and which humans think about differently to the vast network of factual knowledge stored about the category.
People hold remarkably strong beliefs about form properties.

I refer to these as form signatures: beliefs, inferences, or other qualities that are selectively activated for form properties and distinguish them from the broader generic knowledge stored about a category.
For example, form properties are understood as permanent parts of the category, present forever.
People endorse statements like: "even as the properties of restaurants change over time, restaurants will always serve food.
They will be this way forever" (Haward, 2022a).
text.formatted: They will be this way forever" <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Haward, 2022a)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, they believe that architects will always design buildings, that dogs will always bark, that triangles will always have three sides, that watches will always tell time, that weddings will always involve a union of people, and so on.
But they do not endorse this strong belief about generic properties.
They reject that restaurants "will always have wifi," "will always have windows," "will always have pictures on the walls."
This is called the stability signature of central form, a strong belief activated for the central form of each concept, no matter its domain.
Second, people believe that form properties should exist in category members, and there is something wrong with category members that lack a form property.
For example, restaurants should serve food, and there is something categorically wrong with a restaurant that cannot serve food.

But there is nothing categorically wrong with a restaurant if it does not have wifi, windows, pictures on the walls, and so on (called the normative signature; Haward, 2025b; see also Aristotle in Kirby, 2008; Prasada & Dillingham, 2006).

text.text: Finally, form properties are conceived of as universal.

For example, participants will endorse the strong belief that "all restaurants, without exception, serve food," "all architects, without exception, design buildings," and "all watches, without exception, tell time."
They do not endorse equivalent beliefs about the generic properties of these concepts (called the universality signature; Haward, 2025a).

text.text: Evidence suggests these strong beliefs are activated as soon as people have encoded a property as part of the central form of a new concept.

For example, when people learn that having a handle is "part of what makes a blicket a blicket," they immediately endorse the full strong-belief profile (Haward, 2022b (Haward, , 2025a (Haward, , 2025b;; Haward et al., 2021).

text.text: This pattern has been observed across domains, including newly learned animals, artifacts, spaces, institutions, and social categories.
That a set of strong beliefs is activated like this, without being taught, captures a powerful type of one-shot learning (see Figure 2).

text.text: It suggests that a central form is an intrinsic part of new concepts, a structure the mind uses to represent the concept's conceptual-identity information.
All the mind needs to do is encode a property as part of it, then a suite of strong beliefs will be activated.
Crucially, strong central form beliefs are overwhelmingly rejected for the other aspects of a concept's generic knowledge (rejected on 60-80% of trials).

The strong beliefs are rejected even if these non-form properties are highly statistically prevalent / prototypical (e.g., being black for tires), play an important causal role (e.g., having an agent for an actor), or were designed to be in category members (e.g., having music players for bars, being rectangular for TVs, having restrooms for gas stations).

Thus, this approach is differentiated from other approaches to category structure which focus on degrees of statistical prevalence, association, or similarity (e.g., Nosofsky, 1986; Rosch, 1973 Rosch, , 1975) ) or degrees of causal importance (e.g., Ahn et al., 2000). 3 While these other approaches may capture how we reason with our categories in other ways, the strong central form beliefs are only endorsed for a small set of properties, for each concept, that participants believe "makes the thing what it is" (e.g., serving food is one of the things that "makes a restaurant a restaurant"). 4Though related, the notion of form is much broader than contemporary approaches to psychological essentialism which propose a belief in a hidden cause which generates surface level properties, a claim often restricted to living things and/or a subset of categories (Gelman, 2003). 5 An approach to forms, both traditional and contemporary, treats them as a structural component of each new concept, rather than a "stance," "schema" or "belief" that we hold about some categories and not others (Barrett, 2001; Cimpian & Salomon, 2014; Gelman, 2003 Gelman, , 2004)).

text.text: Consistent with this, recent work has demonstrated that of the properties which satisfy an important causal schema for a domain-such as being present from birth for an animal or being intentionally designed for an artifact-only a fraction are encoded as part of the concept's central form.
These properties then have the same status, and activate the same strong beliefs, no matter the domain (called the Common Format Hypothesis; Haward, 2025b).

text.text: Finally, while it may be tempting to think of these as simply "defining" properties, the specific proposals differ substantially.
Consider again the universality and stability form signatures.
These beliefs are surprising precisely because they are typically not justified.

For almost all categories, there exist some members which lack even the most defining properties of the category, such as broken watches which do not tell time and war-torn houses which cannot be lived in (e.g., Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953).

text.text: Further, concepts can change quite markedly over time, both over human history and over conceptual development (for examples of conceptual change see Carey, 1985 Carey, , 2009)).

text.text: And yet, participants do endorse these strong beliefs for form properties, and often at high rates (e.g., 70-90% of trials), and for concepts from every domain so far tested (e.g., animals, artifacts, places, institutions, events, social categories).
In all cases, these three strong beliefs-stability, normativity, universality-align for a small subset of the concept's properties, those that capture its conceptual identity.
This pattern is present early in conceptual development (Haward et al., 2018), and in children crossculturally (Haward & Srinivasan, 2026).

text.text: Thus, central forms are not sets of "necessary and sufficient" conditions for reference-properties that must always be present in an entity in the external world for us to use our concept to pick out that entity in an act of reference (e.g., Locke, 1689 Locke, /1975;; Katz, 1997).

text.text: Instead, each concept's form encodes information and then transforms how we think about that information-i.e., the central form is not primarily a rule for categorizing entities in the world, but a structure that gives selected properties a distinctive belief-generating status.

As such, a good metaphor for thinking about central forms is as conceptual frames that shape how we interpret entities in the world, a view consistent with traditional notions of form (Cudworth, 1731).

text.text: Relatedly, Form Theory distinguishes itself from previous approaches to "defining" vs "characteristic" properties, since this notion of "defining" is largely based on the previous classical notion (e.g., Keil & Batterman, 1984; Smith et al., 1974).

text.text: Thus, these approaches do not propose many of the specific hypotheses adopted within Form Theory.
For example, contemporary empirical approaches to "defining" properties concentrate on measures like categorization, typicality ratings, and property extension judgments.
While these measures capture intriguing phenomena, they are not precise enough to assess a concept's underlying central form.
Consider categorization judgments.
Categorization involves a complex, long-range relationship where a mindexternal entity is referred to using a mind-internal concept (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Categorization involves a complex, long-range relationship where a mindexternal entity is referred to using a mind-internal concept (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Many factors likely influence these judgments (Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953), including whether an entity possesses the generic properties of a concept.

text.text: For instance, black objects are more likely to be categorized as tires than pink objects, assuming all other factors are equal (categorization).
Black tires will be judged as more typical tires than pink tires (typicality).
Additionally, we would expect new tires to be black, not pink (property extension).
However, being black is not what fundamentally makes a tire a tire; it is a generic property of tires.

Focusing on these measures has led some researchers to classify what seem to be form properties (e.g., flying for a bird) as "characteristic," rather than defining, because they do not occur in every member and cannot be said to "define" categorization (e.g., Hampton, 1979; Smith et al., 1974).

text.text: This makes the prediction that, even though they are typically unwarranted, humans will "fall back" on these beliefs when conflicting information is not present (or not processed).

This default-structure proposal plays a crucial role in understanding how humans combine concepts together, and it may go a long way toward understanding many of the biased beliefs we come to hold (again, reviewed in the General Discussion).

It is also in line with early modern and Enlightenment theories of form that took forms to be internal ideals, used primarily for thinking and reasoning, and not perfect descriptions of the external world (e.g., Cudworth, 1731).
If all concepts possess central forms, and if central forms trigger strong beliefs which can shape how we interpret the world, then it is crucial to discover any additional formgenerated beliefs.
Discovering the complete set of form-generated beliefs may help us better understand this structure, its role in human cognition, as well as the errors it can lead to in thinking and reasoning.
The present paper proposes a new form signature-called the certainty signature (call this the Certainty Signature Hypothesis).

According to this hypothesis, the central form is one important source of psychological certainty in the human mind, as concepts are recruited for belief-generation and for interpreting the entities around us, which are almost always viewed through the lens of our concepts.
Specifically, on the Certainty Signature Hypothesis, the central form generates an initial sense of psychological certainty that new category members will possess their form properties.
This signature would seem suited to the roles that categories play.

As we navigate through our environments, we often interact with thousands of new members of different categories in each space we occupy, at each moment (e.g., not just chairs and tables, but insects, lights, pipes, cracks, holes, people of different professions, different categories of hairstyles, different categories of institutions, roads, dwellings, and so on).

According to this hypothesis, while people generalize many of a concept's factual/generic properties to new category members, they exhibit an initial sense of certainty that form properties will exist in newly encountered category members (for examples of generalization tasks, see Gelman, 2003).

text.text: Two clarifications are necessary.
First, it is important to emphasize that it is psychological certainty, and not epistemic certainty, that is being proposed as a new form signature.

As already noted, we often come across category members that lack their form properties, as was thoroughly documented in critiques of early classical approaches to concepts (e.g., Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953).
text.formatted: As already noted, we often come across category members that lack their form properties, as was thoroughly documented in critiques of early classical approaches to concepts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fodor, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Wittgenstein, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: And so, it is patently true that humans do not possess epistemic certainty about most-perhaps any-of the properties that category members actually possess.
Rather, the Certainty Signature Hypothesis proposes that a type of psychological expectation is activated for properties that are part of a concept's central form.

This expectation is likely similar in character to some of the other sources of psychological certainty documented in the literature on certainty (e.g., attitude certainty), which though not justified on epistemic grounds, are felt "with conviction" (Burton, 2009; Tormala & Rucker, 2018).
text.formatted: This expectation is likely similar in character to some of the other sources of psychological certainty documented in the literature on certainty (e.g., attitude certainty), which though not justified on epistemic grounds, are felt "with conviction" <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Burton, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Tormala & Rucker, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, and as a second point of clarification, this psychological certainty can clearly be overridden in particular circumstances, with additional processing of contextual information, memory, pragmatic information, or other case-specific evidence, which will come at a cost.

For example, if a student claims they are certain that a new bird they are learning about in a classroom will fly is then reminded that penguins do not fly, they may revise their certainty belief in that moment.
Alternatively, if someone walks into a watchmaker's store or a museum, they are unlikely to believe with certainty that every new watch they see will tell time.
Thus, this signature has a similar default character to the other form signatures, which are activated, but which can be overridden with case-specific, contextual processing.

This default character of form-generated beliefs makes sense given a cognitive system where conceptual structure is only one factor that determines any judgment or inference, which will of course be the output of many different factors.

It raises interesting questions about when humans may be more likely to fall back on central form beliefs, such as under heavy load or stress, but I leave a discussion of some of the deeper implications of this new form signature for human cognition to the General Discussion.
The primary aim of the present paper is to test a focused prediction of Form Theory, namely that psychological certainty is a signature of central form.
Will participants say they are certain that newly encountered category members will possess their form properties, but uncertain that they will possess their non-form properties?

Given that category members can lack even their most defining properties (e.g., broken or damaged category members), it might seem surprising that people would be willing to say they are certain that category members will possess any of their properties.

Then again, the other form beliefs are strong and often unwarranted, and we often observe psychological certainty expressed in our daily lives, especially in contexts which do not promote contextual or metareflective reasoning (e.g., social media platforms).

To test whether certainty is activated by the central form of each concept, Experiment 1 probed whether participants endorse certainty beliefs for form properties of familiar categories, but not non-form properties.
Experiment 2 then probed more directly whether this strong belief is immediately activated as soon as a property is encoded as part of the central form of a newly learned category.
Experiment 1 tested participants' generalization of form properties and generic properties to new category members.
Both sets of properties were highly generalizable properties of the categories tested.

Experiment 1 tested whether both properties would be generalized to new category members, as in classic generalization tasks (Gelman, 2003; Keil, 1989), but whether participants would only exhibit certainty that form properties would exist in new category members.

At the beginning of the study, participants were told that three researchers had traveled to a city they had not previously visited, and that the researchers' job was to make notes about some of the things they encountered while they explored the city.
Participants were then informed that they would hear about some of the specific encounters of the researchers, and they would be asked some questions.
Trial structure.

On each trial, participants were told about one of the specific entities the researchers had encountered on one of the days they were exploring the city (e.g., "One day, the researchers came across an actor").
They were then asked two test questions about this entity/category member-a presence question and a certainty question.
Both questions were about a potential property the entity/category member might have (e.g., portraying characters).
Presence Question.

On the presence question, participants were asked whether they thought the specific category member would have the property for that trial (e.g., after being told the researchers had met an actor, they were asked: "Do you think they portray characters?"
; yes/no response options).

The presence question is therefore a test of property generalization-whether participants generalize a specific property to a specific category member, given the context of researchers exploring a new city and encountering objects/people/events in that new city.
Certainty Question.
On the certainty question, participants were asked if they were certain that the specific category member encountered would have the property (e.g., "Are you certain that they portray characters?"
; yes/no response options).
6 The presence question was always asked first, followed by the certainty question.
This ordering allowed participants to indicate that they expected the property to be present without also endorsing certainty.
Further, in the certainty question, the word "certain" was bolded and italicized to emphasize the strength of the belief being assessed.
Stimuli.

Participants completed 32 trials, involving 16 categories and two properties per category: a form property (e.g., portraying characters for an actor) and a generic property (e.g., having an agent for an actor).

Experiment 1 tested categories from different domains, since the present paper proposes a hypothesis about the central form of concepts, and the central form is, by hypothesis, part of the structure of concepts from any domain.

Experiment 1 provided evidence in support of the claim that form properties possess a psychological certainty signature.

Participants went beyond simply generalizing a form property to a new category member, to instead indicating that they were certain a form property would be present in a newly encountered category member.
They did not make such a judgment for generic properties.

Many of these generic properties are prototypical for category members (e.g., being black for tires), play an important causal role in category members (e.g., having an agent for an actor), or were designed to be in category members (e.g., having music players for bars, being rectangular for TVs, having restrooms for gas stations).
Further, these generic properties are habitually present in category members, reflected in the high rates of generalization for these properties.
And yet, when asked about a newly encountered category member, participants were only certain that it would possess its form properties, not these generic properties.
In many respects, this is a surprising finding.
In psychology and philosophy, much has been made of the fact that category members often lack the properties that seem to define/identify them (e.g., Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953).

text.text: For example, we encounter watches that do not tell time, and we can still think about them as watches.
And we can encounter houses that are not livable, and we can still think about them as houses.
Crucially, in the present paper we are investigating something quite different to the epistemic certainty discussed in previous theories of conceptual structure.
Rather, Experiment 1 provides evidence for the psychological phenomenon of people feeling certain that form properties will be present in any given category member.
And, of course, the beliefs people hold can be inaccurate.
Experiment 1 suggests that people do indeed possess an initial degree of certainty, all else equal, that the objects they encounter will possess their form properties.

That is, as someone gazes over at a set of chairs and tables outside a café in the distance, they may initially possess an expectation of psychological certainty they will be able to sit on the chairs and place objects on the tables.

Nevertheless, while Experiment 1 demonstrated that this type of psychological certainty tends to be present for form properties, but not for generic properties, it did not demonstrate that this certainty belief is intrinsically tied to the property's status as a form property.
After all, these are familiar categories with which the participants will have had extensive experience.

To investigate whether this is a genuine signature of the central form of human concepts, it is crucial to explore whether this signature follows directly and immediately as soon as a property is encoded as part of a concept's central form, by utilizing a novel category paradigm.
Experiment 2 provides a more direct test of the Certainty Signature Hypothesis.
The aim of Experiment 2 was to test whether the proposed certainty belief is immediately triggered as soon as a property has been encoded as part of the central form of a newly learned category.
In Experiment 2, participants were told that a set of researchers had been exploring a remote island that they had not been to before.

On each trial, participants were told about a novel category the researchers had learned about while on the island (e.g., a place called a "bozon") and they were told about a property of that novel category (e.g., that bozons serve milk).

Importantly, they were either introduced to this property with evidence that it was part of the category's central form, or with evidence that it was generic-licensing, but not part of the central form.
On test, participants were told about a specific encounter the researchers had with a member of each category while exploring the island.
Participants then completed the two test questions from Experiment 1-the presence question and the certainty question.
If the proposed psychological certainty belief is indeed a signature of central form, it should be automatically adopted by participants in the form condition but not in the non-form condition.
This would show that psychological certainty beliefs are intrinsically tied to newly encoded form properties.

Introduction.
Participants were presented with a scenario in which three researchers had traveled to a remote island.
These researchers were interested in studying the animals, artifacts, places and people on the island.
Trial structure.
On each trial, participants were told that on one day, the researchers had encountered some new members of a category (e.g., "On one day, the researchers came across some places called bozons").
They were then told: "Here is what we know so far about bozons," after which they were told about a property that the researchers had learned about (e.g., serving milk).
Participants were either in a form condition or a generic condition.
In the form condition, the property was introduced with evidence that it was part of the central form of the category (e.g., "Serving milk is part of being a Bozon.
It's what makes a bozon a bozon").
In the generic condition, the same property was introduced as true of the category, but not part of its central form (e.g., "Bozons serve milk, but serving milk is not part of being a bozon").
On test, participants were told about different days when the researchers had been exploring the island and encountering specific category members.
Participants then completed the same two test questions used in Experiment 1-the presence question and the certainty question.
For example, for the presence question, they were told that on a different day exploring the island, the researchers came across another bozon.
They were then asked whether they thought the category member would possess the property (e.g., "Do you think that it serves milk?"
; response options yes/no).
Once again, as in Experiment 1, this was followed by the certainty question ("Are you certain that it serves milk?"
; response options yes/no).

As in Experiment 1, this ordering allowed participants to indicate that they expected the property to be present without also endorsing certainty, and the word "certain" was bolded and italicized to emphasize the strength of the belief being assessed.
Stimulus checks.

Stimulus checks confirmed that both introduction frames-the form frame and the generic frame-established the property as true of the category; that both frames led participants to generalize the introduced property to a new category member; that both frames led participants to judge the property as present in category members most of the time; and that both frames led participants to judge the property as causally central.

text.text: The Form Measurement Phase measures whether participants have actually encoded each property as a form property, for each of the four properties they learned about (e.g., serving milk, for a bozon).

At the beginning of the Form Measurement Phase, participants were told that we are now interested in how they were thinking about each of the properties of each of the categories they just learned about.
Then, participants were told (e.g., for bozons) to "Recall that in one of the scenarios you read about a kind of thing called a bozon."
They were then asked: "Did you think that serving milk was part of being a bozon (i.e., one of those things that makes a bozon a bozon)?"
The Form Measurement Phase does not play as crucial a role here as it has in prior studies.

In prior work, it has been used to measure individual differences in which properties people encode as part of the central form of familiar social concepts such as government, country, and religion-for example, whether one person encodes "having a strong leader" as part of what makes a country a country, whereas another encodes "providing public services" as part of what makes a country a country (Haward, 2026b).

text.text: These prior studies highlight that two distinct questions can be asked about form encoding.
First, what cues lead people to encode a property as part of a concept's central form?
There are likely many, including pedagogical cues, linguistic cues, domain-specific biases, and other higher-level constraints (see Haward, 2026a, for discussion).

Given that humans learn tens of thousands of concepts under different circumstances, this will at times lead different people to encode different properties as part of the central form of the same concept.
In prior work, the Form Measurement Phase allowed these differences to be identified.
In contrast, the present study focuses on a second question: what beliefs follow once that encoding has occurred-in this case, psychological certainty.

As noted in the previous section, the present study used relatively neutral properties, as well as a strong linguistic cue to form encoding, which was either included (in the form frame) or not included (in the generic frame).

Experiment 2 provides a key piece of evidence that the proposed certainty signature follows from encoding a property as part of a concept's central form.

Recall that there are two distinct questions about form encoding: first, the cues people use to encode a property as a form property; second, having encoded a property, which beliefs about it immediately follow.
By including clear cues to form encoding, the focus of Experiment 2 is the second of these questions.
It provides evidence that psychological certainty follows immediately once a property is encoded as part of a concept's central form.

As noted in Section 3.1, however, there are likely many routes to form encoding-some more explicit, such as direct linguistic or pedagogical cues, and others more implicit, such as domain-specific biases and other non-linguistic factors-and future work should continue to investigate these possibilities more directly (for further discussion, see Haward, 2026a).

text.text: Finally, while it may seem intuitive-even self-evident-that psychological certainty about a property's possession in future members would follow directly from evidence that a property is part of "what makes an X an X," it is important to acknowledge two points.

First, conceptual identity and certainty about future possession are distinct inferences, and many literatures have been at pains to stress that even for the most seemingly defining properties of categories, we should not be certain of their presence in members (e.g., Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953).
text.formatted: First, conceptual identity and certainty about future possession are distinct inferences, and many literatures have been at pains to stress that even for the most seemingly defining properties of categories, we should not be certain of their presence in members (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fodor, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Wittgenstein, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: Second, a strong intuition like this is exactly what Form Theory would predict, since on this theory conceptual identity and certainty are tightly interlinked (see Section 4.1 for further discussion).
The present paper introduced and provided evidence for a novel signature of central form, called the certainty signature.

On this proposal, people exhibit a default sense of psychological certainty that form properties will be present in category members, which they do not exhibit for the broader generic/factual knowledge they have about the category.

The data suggest that: (i) as soon as a new concept is learned and a property is encoded as part of that concept's central form, this strong certainty belief is immediately activated; (ii) this strong certainty belief remains, even for richly structured, familiar concepts like novel, football game, and actor, which will have been part of these participants' stock of concepts for decades.
In both cases, participants exhibited psychological certainty for the properties that capture the concept's conceptual identity (e.g., what makes a fep a fep, what makes a novel a novel).
They sharply differentiated these form properties from generic/factual properties.

Given the generative nature of human concepts, in the sense that we can form an indefinite number of concepts during our lifetimes which are then used by the systems of the mind for reasoning, planning, and ultimately human action, the present paper raises critical questions: (i) What is the nature of the psychological certainty belief activated by the central form of each human concept?
(ii) Since other systems utilize concepts, what are the consequences for how humans think and reason?
(iii) Why might a mind build in a sense of certainty for a subset of each concept's properties?
(iv) How might this proposal relate to existing research on conceptual representation and psychological certainty?

The current results complement a recent body of work which demonstrates that strong, often unwarranted beliefs are activated as soon as a property is encoded as part of a concept's central form (Haward, 2022b (Haward, , 2025a (Haward, , 2025b)).

text.text: In each case, a qualitative shift occurs in the knowledge acquired about the newly encoded property.
Take the present signature.

By encoding a property as part of a concept's central form, the property goes from being understood as one which will likely exist in its members (on a graded scale), to one which participants are certain will exist in its members (a categorical distinction).

Likewise, the property goes from being understood as persisting in category members temporarily (on a graded scale), to existing in category members forever (a categorical distinction; Haward, 2022b).
text.formatted: Likewise, the property goes from being understood as persisting in category members temporarily (on a graded scale), to existing in category members forever (a categorical distinction; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Haward, 2022b)</ref>.

text.text: And it goes from being understood as existing in some members (on a graded scale), to instead existing in all members (a categorical distinction; Haward, 2025a).

Further, these transitions are "strong" not merely because they are categorical, but because they often involve large inferential jumps-toward certainty, permanence, or universality-that go well beyond the evidence available.
Indeed, as noted in the introduction, people often encounter cases that directly contradict these absolute beliefs, yet still endorse them.
Given the typically unwarranted nature of these form-generated beliefs, it may be tempting to imagine that they are only expressed in the present paradigms.

And yet, extensions of these lines of work show that children and adults exhibit them in culturally and socially rich contexts where their judgments matter for their own lives, exhibit them cross-culturally, and endorse them using other response measures beyond the certain/not certain options used in the present studies (Haward, 2026b; Haward & Srinivasan, 2026).
text.formatted: And yet, extensions of these lines of work show that children and adults exhibit them in culturally and socially rich contexts where their judgments matter for their own lives, exhibit them cross-culturally, and endorse them using other response measures beyond the certain/not certain options used in the present studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Haward, 2026b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Haward & Srinivasan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, when a child in India says that "not eating pork" is part of "what makes a Muslim a Muslim," they are much more likely to report being "completely sure" that a Muslim person they are about to encounter will not eat pork, compared to children who did not see this property as part of what makes a Muslim a Muslim.

The same child will be more likely to believe this is what all Muslims do, that Muslims will continue to not eat pork in the future, and to believe that there is something categorically wrong with a Muslim who does eat pork.

Both Hindu and Muslim children aged 12-15 demonstrate this pattern for a variety of religious concepts (e.g., Hindu, Muslim) and a variety of traits (e.g., "not eating beef/pork," "believing in a deity"), only exhibiting the strong beliefs if they had encoded the property as part of the religious concept's central form, its conceptual identity.

This form-measurement approach also predicts the strong judgments adults possess about socially relevant concepts like government and country, showing that individual differences in the endorsement of strong form-generated beliefs can be predicted by whether any given property (e.g., providing public services, having a strong leader) is seen as part of "what makes a government a government" or "what makes a country a country."

In these lines of work, participants often endorse these beliefs using even stronger language than was used in the present experiment (e.g., "I'm completely certain," "I'm completely sure") and with scales that present other options (e.g., "not sure," "a little sure," "completely sure").

The present work is also consistent with the documentation of psychological certainty beliefs in the political domain, in religious contexts, in memory retrieval, during conflict, as well as in many other domains of life (Burton, 2009; Talarico & Rubin, 2003; Rios et al., 2014; Tormala & Rucker, 2018).

text.text: Form Theory therefore raises the possibility that future research could link some of these deeply held beliefs to the internal structure of our concepts.
A further concern may be that in Experiment 2 participants were directly told about the conceptual identity of each concept ("what makes a fep a fep").
Therefore, isn't it natural they would then be certain the property will exist in any given category member?
Ultimately, this is precisely the point.

This line of work seeks to establish: (i) what logically follows, in the mind, from conceiving of a property in this manner, as part of what makes a fep a fep (strong certainty, stability, normativity, and universality beliefs); (ii) that these strong beliefs are restricted to properties that are part of the concept's conceptual identity, part of its central form; (iii) that this cluster of interrelated strong beliefs continues to be activated for the conceptual identities of familiar concepts like actor, gas station, protest, Hindu, and government (what makes a protest a protest, what makes a government a government).

That this pattern has been shown to be present for all concepts so far tested, both novel and familiar, drawn from many different domains, is strong evidence that each concept possesses a central form that activates these strong (often unwarranted) beliefs.

As is often the case within the sciences-and particularly within a relatively young field like cognitive sciencedifferent approaches to these issues exist, within different frameworks (e.g., Bayesian approaches, causal-model approaches, connectionist approaches; Tenenbaum et al., 2006; Sloman, 2005; Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986).

text.text: For example, an alternative explanation for the results may be that participants' certainty judgments reflect threshold-based processes.
Specifically, participants may estimate the prevalence of properties across category members and report certainty only when these estimates exceed a high threshold (e.g., 90%).
While integrating these results into alternative frameworks may hold independent value, it is critical to consider these data in the broader context of findings on central form.

As noted: (i) a whole cluster of strong beliefs are activated for form properties, not just one; (ii) these strong beliefs are activated immediately, as soon as a property gains the status of a form property; (iii) they are then maintained at high rates for familiar concepts which participants have likely possessed for decades; and (iv) this takes place for all types of concepts, across different domains.
Even within alternative frameworks, these data reveal highly systematic patterns that would need to be integrated and activated should a property pass a designated threshold.

Furthermore, positing a threshold like this for every concept that the mind generates, and proposing that it automatically activates a whole cluster of beliefs, is inherently a proposal about mental structure.
In this sense, the present work holds considerable value for alternative frameworks by providing systematic patterns that any model of conceptual representation and reasoning must explain.
12 Fully differentiating between entire frameworks goes beyond the scope of this paper, and future work may explore these ideas.
13  Form Theory, however, treats the central form as a specific type of structure, part of each concept, which is consistent with historical approaches to form.

It is part of an approach to the mind that considers there to be distinct types of mental representation (e.g., visual representations, linguistic representations…) with distinct structure (e.g., verbs have roles).
This approach to the mind is highly consistent with the rest of biology, which proposes distinct systems and component parts, each with distinct structure.

Form Theory adopts this structural interpretation for concepts and their central forms because central forms display all the empirical hallmarks of a specific type of structure: they are present in concepts early in life and across the lifespan, present in entirely new concepts, remain present as concepts encode more information over time, and are present in concepts from any domain.

Moreover, without learning anything specific about a new kind of thing-say, when hearing a new word in conversation-we likely have the intuition that there is "something about it that makes it what it is."
Systematic patterns like this, although abstract, warrant an explanation.
This too is consistent with the central form being a preexisting structure within each concept, capturing its conceptual identity, but requiring information to be encoded within it.

By characterizing the central form as a distinct structure, Form Theory also makes it possible to ask deeper questions about how this structure functions in thought, including whether it operates as a default mental structure that humans may at times fall back on, subsequently activating strong form-generated beliefs.
12 In the case of a statistical threshold, the threshold would need to either vary by concept or be very high.
In the present study, generic properties like being black were included which are extremely prevalent in category members, well above 90% (consider how often you come across non-black tires).
In fact, across all properties in Experiment 1, the generalization of form properties and generic properties to new members was near identical (98.75% vs 92.66% respectively).
13 One way to approach this question is to ask: Is the threshold inherently statistical?
Three considerations are worth noting.
First, the statistical beliefs activated as part of the suite of form-generated beliefs are internal beliefs that neither accurately reflect the external world nor are graded.

For example, participants accept statements about form properties like "all watches, without exception, tell time" and "all motorcars, without exception, have an engine," even though the external world includes watches and motorcars that lack these properties.

Second, while it is plausible that statistical information plays a role in encoding a property as a form property, many other cues likely contribute, such as pedagogical cues, causal cues, and form-signature cues (e.g., hearing a speaker express certainty that a category member possesses the property).
Third, once encoded, a whole cluster of form-generated beliefs is activated, not all of which are statistical in nature.

In fact, taking the form-generated beliefs together-certainty, permanence, normativity, and universality-the central form may represent our "internal ideals" for each concept, a proposal consistent with traditional approaches to form (Cudworth, 1731).

text.text: But surely form-generated psychological certainty can be overridden?
We can entertain the thought that a particular watch might not tell time, that a particular house might not be livable, and that a particular architect might not be able to design buildings.
Entertaining these thoughts appears to be easiest when salient external causes exist that account for why a category member lacks a form property.
For example, if we visit a watchmaker's store, we are unlikely to be certain that any given watch we encounter will tell time.
Similarly, if we are walking through a war zone, we are unlikely to believe with certainty that any given house we encounter will be livable.

Consistent with this, Form Theory does not claim that form-generated psychological certainty must be rigidly maintained over time. 14 Rather, as noted in the introduction, it is proposed as a type of default belief that can be overridden with additional processing (Figure 8).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, Form Theory does not claim that form-generated psychological certainty must be rigidly maintained over time. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_6">14</ref> Rather, as noted in the introduction, it is proposed as a type of default belief that can be overridden with additional processing (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">8</ref>).

text.text: That is, it provides the mind/brain with an initial expectation in the absence of contradictory contextual information.

The present paper lays the foundations for future lines of work exploring the interplay of these factors, such as the cost associated with bringing in additional context, and the situations in which people may be more likely to fall back on form-generated certainty (e.g., in conflict, under stress, under time pressure; see Section 4.3).
The other form signatures also seem to possess this default character.
For example, central forms impose the normative expectation that category members should possess form properties and there is something wrong with a member lacking a form property.
A watch should tell time, a strawberry should be red, and a bird should be able to fly.
Both adult and child participants make these judgments (including normative judgments about these specific form properties; Haward et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Both adult and child participants make these judgments (including normative judgments about these specific form properties; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Haward et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: But, upon reflection, there is nothing necessarily wrong with a category member that lacks a form property.
There is nothing wrong with a watch that has been taken apart to be cleaned, or an unripe strawberry, or a baby chick.
In these cases, additional causal/contextual knowledge justifies the absence of a form property, and inhibits the default judgment that there is something wrong with the category member.

For each of the form signatures, there appears to be a distinction equivalent to what researchers working on certainty call the psychological/epistemic distinction (between psychological certainty and epistemic certainty; Burton, 2009).
text.formatted: For each of the form signatures, there appears to be a distinction equivalent to what researchers working on certainty call the psychological/epistemic distinction (between psychological certainty and epistemic certainty; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Burton, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Namely, each of these signatures is a psychological expectation, held with conviction by an individual, and so will not always be well justified.
The nature of these signatures, as psychological and default expectations triggered by a concept's central form, suggests interesting avenues for future research.

For example, people often exhibit certainty about their beliefs during conflicts (Rios et al., 2014), during clinical depression (Miranda & Mennin, 2007), and when reflecting on their memories (e.g., Day & Ross, 2014; Hirst et al., 2009).

text.text: The results of the present paper lay the foundations to test, for any expression of psychological certainty in these domains, whether the strong beliefs derive from how a person's concepts have been structured.
Consider, as another example, stereotype representations.
Humans possess a tendency to acquire overly simplified concepts of men, women, Black people, White people, Asians, Mexicans, and so on.
When reasoning using these stereotype representations, people appear to exhibit the psychological signatures of central form, often in a default manner and without adequate justification.
Take the well-documented stereotype of Asians and the trait of being competent at mathematics (e.g., Shih et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Take the well-documented stereotype of Asians and the trait of being competent at mathematics (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Shih et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Future work might explore whether some people-those who hold the stereotype, who have encoded "being good at math" as part of what makes an Asian an Asian-exhibit an initial sense of certainty that any given Asian person they encounter will be good at mathematics.

If the same person (i) believes that Asians should be competent at mathematics, and that they are a "bad Asian" if they are not (ii) believes Asians will be this way forever (iii) expresses that "they're all like that," then this would be strong evidence that these pernicious beliefs arise from human concepts more generally possessing a central form.

Should this be true, it would align with an expanding body of research which suggests that humans have a natural tendency to form and perpetuate stereotypical beliefs (e.g., Cimpian & Markman, 2011; Gelman et al., 2004; Rhodes et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2017; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021).

text.text: Deep questions remain about why human concepts are structured this way.
Why would a cognitive system build into each concept a central structure that imposes such strong beliefs on the information it encodes?
Benefits for Thinking About Local Environments.
One possibility is that when navigating our environments, we encounter thousands of category members at any moment which we need to process to determine whether and how to engage with them.

When walking down the street, we encounter not only roads, cars, and pedestrians, but also dogs, lampposts, crosswalks, chairs and tables, cracks and potholes, banks and cafés, clouds and rain droplets, different kinds of sounds, professions, hairstyles and spaces.
For each concept, we represent a vast number of properties potentially existing in individual members (e.g., for a café, that it will have wifi, places to work, restrooms, chairs and tables).

We surely, at times, process the likelihood that these properties will be present in any category member we are about to encounter (e.g., drawing on statistical, contextual, and pragmatic processing).
But this additional processing will come at a cost, and computation is costly for an organism (Harris et al., 2012; Mink et al., 1981).
text.formatted: But this additional processing will come at a cost, and computation is costly for an organism <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Harris et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Mink et al., 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, if the cognitive system can presume the existence of a small subset of properties for each concept, with certainty, it can offload some of that computational cost.
These certainty judgments will do well much of the time.

For example, if you are walking along the sidewalk and notice a cluster of chairs outside of a café in the distance, it makes sense to presume with certainty that these will allow for sitting, thus preserving computational resources to process the likelihood that the chairs will be comfortable, or whether it will rain soon, or what time the café will close, and so on.
Another possibility is that the existence of a central form within each concept makes distinctively human thought computationally tractable (Haward, 2022a (Haward, , 2025c; Figure 9).
text.formatted: Another possibility is that the existence of a central form within each concept makes distinctively human thought computationally tractable <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Haward, 2022a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Haward, , 2025c</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure">9</ref>).

text.text: Humans can combine concepts at a rapid rate in thought and language to produce complex structures of a length and complexity unimaginable by any other species on Earth (100-200 words are combined in a typical minute of speech; Chafe, 2015; Yuan et al., 2006).

text.text: Since each concept stores such a vast amount of generic/factual information, even simple combinations are consistent with hundreds of meanings.
For example, the sentence/thought "the restaurant was efficient" does not specify which property of the restaurant was efficient.

Is it the restaurant's restrooms, plumbing, electricity, overhead lighting, air conditioning, or any of the many other properties understood as part of our generic knowledge of restaurants and often present in restaurants?

In Haward (2022a), people showed a striking preference for form interpretations, interpreting sentences in terms of form properties 80-90% of the time (in this case, interpreting the sentence to mean that the restaurant's serving of food was efficient, one of those properties that makes a restaurant a restaurant).
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Haward (2022a)</ref>, people showed a striking preference for form interpretations, interpreting sentences in terms of form properties 80-90% of the time (in this case, interpreting the sentence to mean that the restaurant's serving of food was efficient, one of those properties that makes a restaurant a restaurant).

text.text: This tendency is present (i) when concepts are recruited and combined from any domain (e.g., concepts for artifacts, social agents, animals, events, natural objects, places, and so on); (ii) as soon as a new concept is learned and a property is encoded as part of its central form.
Most revealingly, (iii) participants go as far as to say that non-form interpretations are impossible if sentences are presented without context.
This supports the hypothesis that the central form is a default structure which when combined yields a set of default interpretations.

These are essentially available for free-since form information is represented with certainty and permanence-while non-form interpretations may require additional contextual support before they are deemed possible.

Finally, (iv) when participants are asked to generate their own interpretations of sentences, they spontaneously generate form interpretations, and the properties they include in their interpretations are the exact same ones that, on separate questions, participants express "complete certainty" will exist in members, and which they report will be part of the concept "forever."
This supports the hypothesis that people do indeed fall back on stable, certain central forms when interpreting sentences.
Within Form Theory, this proposal is called Form Composition.
Form composition provides a deep explanation for linguistic creativity.
Markedly different concepts, like person and mountain, drawn from different conceptual domains, can be combined quite naturally to produce an interpretation.

Since the mind prioritizes combining the central forms of each concept, it strips away the "generic/factual noise" and provides interpretations like the person's body (a form property of the concept person) is tall (a form property of the concept mountain; Haward, 2025c).

Further, form composition generates interpretations not only for familiar metaphors (e.g., "The person is a mountain"), but also newly created metaphors (e.g., "The cow is a megaphone," "Her hair is a pancake," "The ballerina is a feather").

More generally, while the causal structure and generic/factual details will differ radically by domain, the central form provides a common format, present within every concept, which can be quickly and easily combined in language and thought.

By representing most of the concept's information in an uncertain manner, and restricting certainty beliefs to a central core of information, the process of combining concepts together is greatly simplified, computationally less costly, and will do well most of the time, with specifications of non-form interpretations of sentences possible with additional linguistic markers, or with the additional processing of contextual cues.

text.text: The entities in the world are massively complex.
Consequently, each concept we learn stores a large body of rich world knowledge.
And yet, we are able to recruit these concepts and rapidly engage in combinatorial, categorical, symbolic thought all the time (Panel 1).
This creates a problem for composition, since even combining two concepts together generates a vast search space of potential meanings (Panel 2).

On the Form Composition Hypothesis, each concept has a central form: a unitary structure that represents a compressed subset of the concept's information in a stable, certainty-generating format (Panel 3).
The central form has a common format and is present in all concepts (Panel 4), including as soon as a new concept is acquired (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: The central form has a common format and is present in all concepts (Panel 4), including as soon as a new concept is acquired (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Because form-encoded information is available by default, it is effectively "presumed," and because the central form is a distinct representational unit, composition can use a simple rule: combine forms (Panel 5).
While this helps make composition tractable by generating default interpretations at minimal cost, it can also lead to reductive and distorted beliefs (Panel 6).

text.text: On this view, humans face at least two related pressures.

First, we must construct some relatively stable and certain reality in a world that, behind the veil of our conceptual structure, is marked by impermanence and complexity (Harvey, 2013; Siderits, 2021).
text.formatted: First, we must construct some relatively stable and certain reality in a world that, behind the veil of our conceptual structure, is marked by impermanence and complexity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Harvey, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Siderits, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, even within what we do conceive, life has become increasingly complex as societies have expanded in scale and organization (Tainter, 1988; Schwartz, 2004).
text.formatted: Second, even within what we do conceive, life has become increasingly complex as societies have expanded in scale and organization <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Tainter, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Schwartz, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Form Theory proposes that one way the mind may counter these destabilizing pressures is by drawing on form structurefoot_8 -which naturally activates certainty, stability, and normative guidance-and encoding more beliefs with that structure.
text.formatted: Form Theory proposes that one way the mind may counter these destabilizing pressures is by drawing on form structure<ref type="foot" target="#foot_8">foot_8</ref> -which naturally activates certainty, stability, and normative guidance-and encoding more beliefs with that structure.

text.text: In line with this, recent work suggests that when children encode more beliefs as part of the central forms of important worldview-organizing concepts, they then view those concepts as playing a more stabilizing and protective role in their lives.

For example, among children in India who share a religious faith, those who encode a broader range of beliefs and practices as part of what makes that religion what it is (i.e., its central form) (i) display the full range of form signatures for those specific beliefs and practices and, crucially, (ii) are considerably more likely to report that their religion makes them feel safe and secure in an uncertain world where bad things can happen (Haward & Srinivasan, 2026).

text.text: This suggests that form-generated beliefs may not only help solve cognitive problems, but may also help satisfy deeper existential needs.

More broadly, it raises the possibility that strongly held beliefs about religion, nation, political identity, social status, family, and other identity-bearing concepts may partly arise when deep needs for stability, certainty, and guidance about how to act lead people to encode more worldview-organizing content in form.

As already noted, different people may encode different properties as part of a concept's central form, and this may partly explain why psychological certainty is expressed for different beliefs across individuals (see Sections 3.1 and 4.1).

But this raises a further question: once an initial default sense of certainty has been generated by the central form of a concept, do people and contexts differ in how readily that certainty is overridden?
There are at least two broad cases in which this question arises.
First, the context may be such that other reflective systems are not even activated, allowing formgenerated beliefs to dominate by default-as appears to be the case in the present experiments.

In everyday life, this may occur in contexts that do not encourage reflective reasoning, such as fast-paced social media environments built around brief, bite-sized responses, or when environmental or habitual factors tax other cognitive systems, such as when people are making decisions quickly, under stress, or with too little sleep.
Under such conditions, the processes required to override form-generated beliefs may not be activated at all.

Second, there may be cases in which the conditions are, in principle, ideal for revision, and yet people still cling to form-generated beliefs-such as psychological certainty about a belief-even when they have time to reflect, recruit other cognitive systems, and consider competing information.
Why might this be?
The answer likely lies in the particular functional roles the signatures of form are serving for that individual in that situation.
Recall that Form Theory places no fixed limit on the number of benefits these signatures may provide for the human mind.

Central forms are proposed to be intrinsic to human concepts and to activate a family of automatic beliefs, but, as noted in the previous section, there are many ways in which systems -and, more broadly, people-may utilize them.
Consider the role form plays in complex thought.
There, form may help massively restrict the initial hypothesis space of sentence meanings.

In that context, readily revising an initial default assumption in light of further evidence, such as new referents in context or pragmatic information, may often be the most rational response, particularly when little depends on maintaining that assumption.

By contrast, if for some beliefs form plays an important stabilizing role by providing people with a sense of certainty and structure within their social frameworks for understanding the world, then the costs of abandoning these beliefs may be much higher, especially when they are foundational and support a wider hierarchy of commitments.

In such cases, even when other cognitive systems can in principle be activated to override form-generated beliefs, people may nevertheless cling to them because of the other functional roles they play.
Understanding the interaction of these factors may motivate a new line of research on when and why humans fall back on form-generated beliefs.
Indeed, Form Theory predicts that, as social life becomes more complex, people may come to express more of their beliefs with certainty.
Under these conditions, both of the pressures described above may intensify.

First, greater numbers of choices, demands, and competing sources of information may increase the frequency with which people operate under conditions that tax reflective systems (Roetzel, 2019), leading to greater reliance on form-generated beliefs and, with them, greater expressions of certainty.

text.text: Second, as traditional social and civic frameworks fragment (Putnam, 2000), people may come to rely more heavily on the other functions of form in establishing certainty, stability, and guidance within their broader belief systems.
