text.text: On this view, Form Theory may help explain a seemingly paradoxical pattern.

Even as people gain access to more information, and so more opportunities to consult alternative perspectives, they do not always respond with more measured reflection, but often with greater certainty.

Further, Form Theory predicts that these effects should be most visible in contexts where complexity, time pressure, stress, and cognitive load make reflective systems less likely to be recruited, including on social media platforms, during political or institutional crises, during public-health emergencies, and in other situations where people must respond quickly to complex and uncertain information.
Form Theory offers a set of specific proposals about the structure of human concepts.

Each concept contains a single, unitary, preexisting central form: a compressed format that stores a subset of conceptual information, provides a common structure across domains, activates strong default beliefs that make sense given its proposed structure and role, and can be recruited by other cognitive systems.
Because this format is recruitable by other systems, it can support powerful computations in thought and language, yielding distinctive benefits for cognition.
At the same time, because the beliefs it activates are default, simplified, and often unwarranted, the same structure can also generate characteristic costs.
These claims, taken together, constitute the distinctive core of Form Theory.

These commitments raise questions about how Form Theory relates to other theories of conceptual representation, especially approaches that emphasize causal structure, domain-specific knowledge, and the distinction between type concepts and concepts of individual entities.

As with other major approaches to concepts-such as prototype theories (e.g., Rosch, 1975; Rosch & Mervis, 1975), definitional theories (e.g., Smith et al., 1974; Katz, 1997), theory-theory approaches (e.g., Murphy & Medin, 1985; Gopnik & Meltzoff, 1997), and causal approaches (e.g., Sloman et al., 1998; Ahn et al., 2000)the central explanatory target is the vast class of type concepts humans acquire, likely numbering in the tens of thousands across development (e.g., Bloom, 2000).

text.text: Form Theory is therefore already a broad theory of concepts, and in some respects broader than approaches focused on natural kinds, since it is intended to apply to all concepts, including artifacts, mathematical concepts, abstract ideas, events, places, institutions, occupations, political identities, and even concepts with temporary application, such as phase sortals.
For example, watch, triangle, democracy, wedding, restaurant, government, architect, nationalist, and passenger all appear to possess forms and to activate form signatures.

More broadly, the pressures that motivate this frameworksuch as the need to compress large amounts of information into a small usable set, and to represent that set in a format suited for composition-are not unique to any narrow class of concepts.
One particularly important point of contact is with causal approaches.
Form Theory does not suggest that the central form replaces domain-specific causal knowledge.
Rather, it suggests that a subset of causally or functionally privileged information from different domains may be extracted and encoded into a common format for thought and language.
Indeed, in novel category studies of the type introduced in Experiment 2, domain-specific knowledge has been shown to play a role in which properties are encoded as form properties.
But crucially, a property only activates form signatures if it has been encoded as a form property (Haward, 2025b).

This view is further supported by evidence that the central form provides a common format that can be rapidly combined across domains, despite large differences in their underlying causal structure (Haward, 2022a).

Further, since central forms are proposed as a default structure, it is possible that people preferentially recruit the form properties of the entities they are reasoning about when constructing causal models, making those properties more likely to occupy important causal roles in those models.
This possibility is consistent with the body of work on form composition, which suggests that central forms are recruited as defaults when concepts are combined.
It may help explain some of the biased reasoning discussed in Section 4.1, if, at times, traits of social groups become form-encoded.

If, for example, aggression is encoded into the central form of a social group concept, people may then be more likely to treat aggression as an explanatory cause when interpreting an event involving a member of that group.
Fully integrating these findings into causal and other existing frameworks of conceptual representation goes beyond the scope of the present paper, but it is an important direction for future work.

A further question is how Form Theory interfaces with concepts of individuals (e.g., Blok et al., 2005), which may operate differently in some respects, but which may nevertheless come to exhibit some of the same signatures of form as knowledge about them accumulates-for example, in judgments such as "I'm certain Mary will behave that way," "Mary always does that," or "That's just who Mary is."

text.text: 17 Form Theory differs from psychological essentialism in at least six ways.
(1) Scope: Form Theory proposes a structure within all concepts, rather than focusing primarily on biological or natural kinds and extensions to social kinds.
(2) Cognitive type: Form Theory is a theory of representational structure, whereas psychological essentialism is typically studied as a theory of essentialist beliefs, construals, or schemas.
(3) Outputs: Form Theory focuses on domain-neutral signatures such as certainty, permanence, normativity, universality, and possibility/impossibility.

In psychological essentialism, some of these outputs have not been studied, such as certainty and possibility/impossibility; some appear similar but measure a different construct, such as the stability of an individual through transformation rather than permanence beliefs about category structure; and others are domain-specific, such as biological inferences about inheritance.

(4) Cognitive utility: Form Theory explains how compressed conceptual structure supports conceptual combination, creativity, analogy, guided attention, and the formation of stable worldview frameworks; psychological essentialism primarily explains how essence-based construals support categorization, induction, and explanation, especially for biological, natural, and social kinds.

(5) Internal structure: Because Form Theory is a theory of representational structure, it has begun to characterize the internal structure of central forms in greater detail, as a set of roles that can accept filler properties (see Haward, 2026a, for detail).
Psychological essentialism, by contrast, primarily characterizes beliefs about hidden essences and the inferences those beliefs support.

(6) Position: Form Theory proposes central form as a default structure within cognitive architecture, with default outputs that can be overridden by other cognitive systems, and places forms, and therefore concepts, at the interface of combinatorial thought and non-linguistic cognition.
Psychological essentialism does not make these architectural claims.
As noted, the present account is not intended to explain every instance of psychological certainty, but rather to reveal a natural expression of our conceptual structure.
Even so, by identifying a possible representational source of certainty, Form Theory may lead to new questions about how this source relates to previously identified sources of certainty.

For example, because form-encoded information acquires the status of default conceptual knowledge, it may be easier to retrieve, processed more fluently, experienced as more coherent, and accompanied by a pre-reflective "feeling of rightness"-factors that have each been linked to increased subjective certainty or confidence (e.g., Schwarz et al., 1991; Reber et al., 2004; Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Koriat, 2012; Thompson et al., 2011).

After all, form-generated certainty, belief stability, and normative understanding-which includes instructions for how we should act-are intrinsically connected within the present framework.
This would be in line with the broader view developed in Section 4.2: that form helps establish stable, guiding frameworks for understanding and navigating the world.

text.text: The present paper is one contribution to this broader literature.
The present account helps resolve a classic puzzle about concepts.

It aligns with critiques of the classical theory of concepts, which correctly argued that there are few, if any, properties we can be epistemically certain will be possessed by category members (e.g., Fodor, 1998; Wittgenstein, 1953).

text.text: We often encounter houses that are not livable, watches that do not tell time, and birds that do not fly.

Nevertheless, Form Theory argues that these concepts still possess a central form, with a suite of distinctive signatures, including the activation of a default psychological certainty belief about the information encoded within that form.
In this way, Form Theory preserves the central insight of the anticlassical critique while showing how concepts can still contain a privileged internal boundary.
The present work shows that it is not only fools and fanatics who possess certainty about their beliefs (cf. Russell, 1933).
text.formatted: The present work shows that it is not only fools and fanatics who possess certainty about their beliefs (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Russell, 1933)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, psychological certainty enters deeply into how we conceive of the entities that structure our lives.
Complementing recent proposals, the present paper reveals another benefit of concepts possessing a central form.
It allows the human mind to presume the existence of some properties of the entities we encounter, which much of the time will be correct.

In going beyond mere likelihood, and in fixing these properties as certainly present, this signature of form may help the mind preserve cognitive resources, support the rapid construction of complex thoughts, and establish stable, guiding frameworks for understanding the world.
And yet, it may also introduce misplaced certainty into some of these beliefs, particularly within the complex, cognitively taxing environments of modern life.
Future research should aim to test these ideas more directly, exploring both the benefits and potential costs of the mind falling back on the central form in thinking and reasoning.
Finally, by approaching psychological certainty through a broader theory of conceptual structure, we can see more clearly why it occupies such a deep place within human cognition.
